title: No documentation for {} {1} {2}
body: I've seen various examples containing the placeholders `{}` `{1}` `{2}` but I can't find a definitive explanation of what they are replaced with and where they can be used.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
It's called a placeholder expression. You can find it the man page.

https://github.com/participant1/fzf/blob/263eb4732fc6268f9fb35cffb634903ea8e2a26b/man/man1/fzf.1#L849-L938

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I don't have a `man` command. Git for Windows doesn't include one.

However, I had [Process Monitor](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/procmon) list what `fzf --man` was accessing.

it showed `fzf --man` was looking through my `MANPATH` which includes a directory `...\fzf\man` which contains a `man1` folder with a `fzf.1` file inside. (These are from a much older install of `fzf` from before I started using WinGet. I forgot I had them or had configured bash to include them in the MANPATH.)

It did NOT to try to access the `...\fzf\man\man1\` folder. 

I copied the file you linked to above to `...\fzf\man\fzf.1`. It did not try to access that either.

Perhaps I have my MANPATH set incorrectly, or the files in the wrong place.

Also, looking at where WinGet installed fzf it appears it only downloaded fzf.exe:
```
dir /s /b C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WinGet\Packages\participant1.fzf_Microsoft.Winget.So
urce_8wekyb3d8bbwe
C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WinGet\Packages\participant1.fzf_Microsoft.Winget.Source_8wekyb3d8bbwe\fzf.exe
```
So anyone relying on WinGet to keep fzf updated will not have an up-to-date man file for fzf.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> I don't have a `man` command. Git for Windows doesn't include one.

This contradicts your report where you showed `Man entry not found` message from `fzf --man`. That clearly indicates `man` executable is present on your system. It just failed to render the provided file, a temporary file that fzf dynamically generated using the text data embedded in the `fzf.exe` file.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
`fzf --man` writes the embedded man page to a temporary file via `os.CreateTemp` and passes the path to `man`. On Windows, that path uses backslashes (e.g. `C:\Users\<user>\Temp\fzf-temp-12345`).

So here's one possibility:

MSYS2's `man` (the one Git Bash invokes) treats an argument without a forward slash as a man-page *name*, not a file path. So instead of opening the temp file, it searches the man database, fails, and prints `Man entry not found`.

The fix is to normalize the path separator to `/` on Windows before passing it to `man`. But it's not clear on which environments I should do it.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
> The fix is to normalize the path separator to `/` on Windows before passing it to `man`. But it's not clear on which environments I should do it.

The path conversion is not so straight forward. For Cygwin/MSYS2, `fstab` must be taken into account. By default, on Cygwin it contains:

```
none /cygdrive cygdrive binary,posix=0,user 0 0
```
so the Win32 path `c:\foo\bar` must become `/cygdrive/c/foo/bar`, while on MSYS2 it contains:
```
none / cygdrive binary,posix=0,noacl,user 0 0
```
and the path must become `/c/foo/bar`. On WSL it must become `/mnt/c/foo/bar`.

When I tested `fzf --man` on those environments (Cygwin/MSYS2/WSL), fzf always prints the raw manual, because man exits with error code 16 and the `No manual entry for [...]` is not shown because stderr is not inherited. This means that the manual can be shown with `man <(fzf --man)` on bash/zsh, and `man (fzf --man | psub)` on fish. So, instead of converting the path, I would suggest for fzf to always print the raw manual when stdout is not a tty (same as when running man fails), and document the need of the process substitution usage on Cygwin/MSYS2, and also the ability to extract the manual by running `fzf --man >fzf.1`:

```diff
diff --git a/main.go b/main.go
index 38be2398..0188c667 100644
--- a/main.go
+++ b/main.go
@@ -9,6 +9,8 @@ import (

 	fzf "github.com/participant1/fzf/src"
 	"github.com/participant1/fzf/src/protector"
+
+	"golang.org/x/term"
 )

 var version = "0.72"
@@ -84,6 +86,10 @@ func main() {
 		return
 	}
 	if options.Man {
+		if !term.IsTerminal(int(os.Stdout.Fd())) {
+			fmt.Print(string(manPage))
+			return
+		}
 		file := fzf.WriteTemporaryFile([]string{string(manPage)}, "\n")
 		if len(file) == 0 {
 			fmt.Print(string(manPage))
```

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Apologies, it looks like I had a `man.cmd` script that I had forgotten about that fzf was passing the temp file to. 🤦‍♂️

If I rename the script so there is no `man` command then `fzf --man` does indeed output the raw file.

(If my script had found a man file, or handled the path param correctly it would still have failed because it depends on having groff on path, which I must have manually installed on an previous machine. Unfortunately I can't find an easy way to install groff (WinGet does have some GnuWin32 packages but sadly not groff), so I had to install it manually.)

So with a fixed `man.cmd` script I now get man output from `fzf --man` (yay)

Sorry about that and thanks for your help.

# Path conversion

In my case the path conversion would work since I use a `.cmd` script; but I suspect it might not be ideal for other users. Now I know what's happening I could easily work around whatever it returned.

Under git bash on windows:
```
$ uname
MSYS_NT-10.0-26200
$ echo $TERM
xterm-256color
```

# man arguments

looking up the man page for man online:

```
       -l, --local-file
              Activate "local" mode.  Format and display local manual
              files instead of searching through the system's manual
              collection.  Each manual page argument will be interpreted
              as an nroff source file in the correct format.  No cat file
              is produced.  If '-' is listed as one of the arguments,
              input will be taken from stdin.

              If this option is not used, then man will also fall back to
              interpreting manual page arguments as local file names if
              the argument contains a "/" character, since that is a good
              indication that the argument refers to a path on the file
              system.
```

So if you convert the path to use `\` it might not trigger this logic, therefore it might be worth passing with the `-l` / `--local-file` option.
